messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus, a 50-year-old African American plumber, had always taken pride in his work, a dependable man whose hands could fix almost anything. That changed six months ago. He was working late in a dimly lit commercial building, deep in the maze of its basement, when a burst pipe demanded his expertise. He heard a scuffle, turned, and was suddenly ambushed by two men who stole his tools and wallet, leaving him battered and shaken. The attack was swift and brutal, a blur of motion and fear. He still vividly sees the glint of metal, the sudden shove, the faces of his attackers, but the exact sequence of events, what he said or did, remains fragmented, difficult to articulate into a coherent narrative.

In the immediate aftermath, a profound sense of injustice consumed him. What happened was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done to apprehend his attackers. This festered alongside an intense guilt, replaying the moments in his mind, certain he should have reacted differently, that he should have been able to defend himself. He had always been a capable man, a skilled tradesman, but now he felt profoundly diminished, convinced he was no longer capable of handling the unexpected, of doing the demanding physical work that had defined him for decades.

This pervasive belief that he was no longer capable, coupled with the deep-seated sense of injustice, fueled a constant undercurrent of dread. He became hyper-alert, especially when working alone or in unfamiliar places. He found himself feeling safe only in a very limited number of places—his home, his workshop, and nowhere else. Any unexpected movement nearby, a sudden shadow shifting in his peripheral vision, or a door creaking open while he was on a job, would send a jolt of alarm through him, causing him to react as if he were in immediate danger. This constant state of vigilance left him utterly exhausted, yet sleep became an elusive comfort, plagued by trouble falling or staying asleep.

When the visual memories of the assault—the faces, the glint of metal, the feeling of being overwhelmed—flashed into his mind, they were accompanied by an overwhelming, corrosive guilt. He couldn't seem to put the frightening event into words, which only amplified his distress and made the experience feel more alien and terrifying. These intrusive visual memories would immediately trigger his body's alarm system, making his heart race, his muscles tense, and leaving him feeling profoundly unsafe and on edge, further intensifying his trouble falling or staying asleep.

The chronic state of hypervigilance, the constant scanning for danger, and the severe sleep problems made it even harder for Marcus to process the traumatic event. His mind, perpetually on guard and exhausted, couldn't settle to organize the fragmented, visual memories into a cohesive narrative. This meant the event remained a jumble of frightening images and sensations, reinforcing his feeling of guilt and his inability to make sense of what happened, preventing him from ever truly putting it behind him.

His plumbing business, once a source of pride and purpose, now felt like a minefield. He started refusing jobs in basements or dimly lit commercial properties, claiming he was too busy, though in truth, he was terrified. His marriage to Clara, once a bedrock of unwavering support, became strained as he withdrew, irritable from lack of sleep and consumed by his internal struggles. He avoided social gatherings, preferring the limited sanctuary of his home. He constantly doubted his own judgment, plagued by self-doubt that he wouldn't do the right thing if confronted with danger again, which only intensified his need to avoid any potential threat.

The cycle had tightened its grip, leaving Marcus feeling trapped. His wife, Clara, eventually insisted he seek help, unable to watch him suffer in silence any longer. He came in, a tired man, plagued by the vivid, silent pictures of his assault, the gnawing guilt, and the pervasive feeling that the world was no longer a safe place. He hoped to find a way to silence the constant alarm bells ringing in his mind and to rediscover the capable man he once was, before the world around him became so terrifyingly unpredictable.
